title: DID GOD APPROVE OF SOLOMON’S 700 WIVES? THE ANSWER IS MORE DISTURBING—AND MORE PERSONAL—THAN YOU THINK
paragraphs:
DID GOD APPROVE OF SOLOMON’S 700 WIVES? THE ANSWER IS MORE DISTURBING—AND MORE PERSONAL—THAN YOU THINK
The Bible never says God approved Solomon’s many wives. It says almost the exact opposite. But buried beneath Solomon’s scandal is a warning about the human heart—and a trail of grace that eventually leads us to Jesus Christ.
Imagine standing inside Solomon’s palace.

Gold catches the light everywhere. Servants move through enormous halls. Foreign dignitaries wait for an audience with the man whose wisdom has become legendary. Kings know his name. Nations have heard of his wealth. The Queen of Sheba herself will marvel at what God has allowed him to possess.
And somewhere behind those palace doors is something almost impossible to comprehend.
Hundreds of women.
Wives.
Concubines.
Political alliances.
Relationships multiplied beyond anything resembling the marriage covenant we see established at creation.
Then comes the uncomfortable question Christians sometimes hesitate to ask:
If Solomon was blessed by God…
if Solomon was given extraordinary wisdom by God…
if Solomon built the Temple…
if Solomon was king over God’s covenant people…
did God approve of all those wives?
No.
And Scripture is remarkably clear about it.
The tragedy is that Solomon possessed enough wisdom to recognize the danger while apparently becoming unable—or unwilling—to escape it himself.
That should frighten us a little.
Because Solomon’s story is not merely about ancient polygamy.
It is about what happens when a person can recognize truth intellectually while slowly negotiating with it personally.
And perhaps that is why his story can feel uncomfortably familiar.
You can know Scripture…
and still compromise.
You can teach truth…
and still hide something.
You can have influence…
and still have idols.
You can appear tremendously blessed…
while something inside your heart is quietly drifting away from the One who blessed you.
Long before Solomon was born, God had already given Israel instructions concerning its future kings.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says in Hebrew:
“וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים, וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ”
Ve-lo yarbeh-lo nashim, ve-lo yasur levavo.
A careful sense of the words is:
“He shall not multiply wives for himself, so that his heart does not turn aside.”
Read that again.
God did not merely warn Israel’s king about pagan worship after the fact.
God warned him about the road that could take his heart there.
Do not multiply wives.
Why?
“וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ”
So that his heart will not turn aside.
The Hebrew word levavo refers to his heart—his inner person, his will, his allegiance.
God was protecting something deeper than Solomon’s reputation.
God was guarding his heart.
And then, generations later, Solomon did almost exactly what the Torah had warned Israel’s king not to do.
First Kings 11 records the devastating result.

Solomon loved many foreign women. The issue in that chapter is not ethnicity, as though Scripture were teaching racial superiority. The text itself identifies the spiritual danger: these relationships involved peoples whose gods could draw Israel into idolatry, and Solomon eventually participated in that idolatry.
The king who should have guarded covenant faithfulness accumulated seven hundred royal wives and three hundred concubines.
One thousand women.
But the number is not even the darkest sentence in the story.
The darkest sentence concerns what happened to his heart.
The Hebrew text of 1 Kings 11:3 says:
“וַיַּטּוּ נָשָׁיו, אֶת־לִבּוֹ”
Vayyattu nashav et-libbo.
His wives turned—or inclined—his heart.
The warning of Deuteronomy had become Solomon’s biography.
God had said that multiplying wives could turn the king’s heart.
Solomon multiplied wives.
And his heart turned.
That is not divine approval.
That is divine warning followed by human disobedience followed by devastating consequences.
We need to understand something important when reading Scripture.
The Bible records many things it does not endorse.
Description is not automatically prescription.

When Scripture tells us that Abraham, Jacob, David, Solomon, and others had multiple wives or concubines, the existence of those relationships in the narrative does not mean God was presenting them as His ideal.
The Bible is brutally honest about its heroes.
That honesty is actually one reason Scripture feels so unlike religious propaganda.
Its greatest human figures are not airbrushed.
Noah becomes drunk.
Abraham acts out of fear.
Jacob deceives.
Moses disobeys.
David commits adultery and orchestrates a man's death.
Peter denies Jesus.
Solomon becomes entangled in idolatry.
The Bible does not need flawless human heroes because the Bible is moving toward a flawless Savior.
And when we return to the beginning, before kings, kingdoms, political marriages, concubines, harems, and royal compromises, the pattern of marriage is strikingly simple.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ, וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
Ve-davaq be-ishto, ve-hayu le-vasar echad.
A man is joined to his wife, and they become “one flesh.”
One covenant union.
And centuries later, when Jesus is questioned about marriage, He does something profoundly important.
He goes backward.
Not merely to Israel’s kings.
Not merely to Moses.
Back to creation.
In Matthew 19, Jesus recalls that the Creator made humanity male and female and speaks of the two becoming one flesh.
The Greek expression is:
“οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν”
hoi dyo eis sarka mian—
“the two into one flesh.”
Then Christ says they are no longer two, but one flesh.
Jesus points His listeners toward God’s creational design.
So no, Solomon’s thousand relationships do not overturn Genesis.
Solomon is not the standard.
Creation is the pattern, and Christ Himself directs us back toward it.
But there is another question hiding underneath all this.
Why would the wisest man alive do something so foolish?
Maybe because wisdom possessed is not necessarily wisdom obeyed.
And now Solomon stops being merely an ancient king.
Now he becomes a mirror.
Because some of us know exactly what God says too.
We know that relationship is pulling us away from Christ.
We know that habit is poisoning us.
We know what happens every time we open that private browser.
We know that bitterness is becoming hatred.
We know that secret conversation with someone who is not our spouse has crossed emotional boundaries.
We know that money has become more than provision—it has become identity.
We know applause has become addictive.
We know pride is controlling us.
We know the Holy Spirit has been pressing the same conviction into our conscience again and again.
Yet somewhere inside ourselves we whisper:
Just one more time.
It isn't that serious.
I can control it.
God understands.
Nobody knows.
I still pray.
I still go to church.
I still post Bible verses.
I still believe.
So did Solomon.
That is what makes his fall terrifying.
This was not a man who had never encountered God.
According to 1 Kings 11, God had appeared to Solomon twice.
Think about that.
Solomon did not fall because he lacked evidence that God existed.
He fell while possessing extraordinary revelation.
And perhaps one of the most dangerous lies a believer can embrace is the idea that yesterday’s encounter with God guarantees tomorrow’s obedience to God.
It does not.
A powerful testimony cannot replace present surrender.
Yesterday’s tears cannot substitute for today’s repentance.
Yesterday’s obedience cannot sanctify today’s compromise.
Solomon’s decline also appears to have happened over time.
That is usually how hearts drift.
Few people wake up and announce, “Today I will destroy my spiritual life.”
It begins smaller.
A boundary moved.
A warning rationalized.
A conviction delayed.
A secret protected.
An appetite fed.
Another compromise.
Then another.
Until eventually the thing you once controlled begins controlling you.
Sin rarely introduces itself by saying, “I have come to ruin you.”
It usually whispers, “You deserve this.”
Solomon “clung” to these women in love.
That detail matters.
Because something can feel deeply emotional and still be spiritually destructive.
Something can feel like love while competing with your love for God.
Something can feel impossible to surrender while becoming the very thing Christ is asking you to place in His hands.
And here is where this story becomes painful.
Maybe your “many wives” are not people.
Maybe they are the many little loyalties competing for your heart.
The approval you cannot live without.
The money you cannot stop chasing.
The lust nobody sees.
The resentment you secretly rehearse.
The relationship you know is pulling you from Christ.
The status you worship.
The ministry platform that quietly became more important than the God you were supposedly serving through it.
The image of yourself you are terrified to lose.
Your heart has only one throne.
And anything we love more than Christ eventually becomes a cruel master.
That is why Solomon’s story cannot simply end with us shaking our heads at Solomon.
We need to ask the question we would rather avoid:
What is turning my heart?
Not what turned Solomon’s.
Mine.
What have I been calling harmless that God has been calling dangerous?
What have I been defending because surrender would hurt?
What warning have I repeatedly heard but quietly ignored?
Be honest.
This may be hitting harder than you expected.
Maybe you look completely fine to everyone around you.
Maybe people come to you for encouragement.
Maybe you can explain doctrine.
Maybe you know verses by memory.
Maybe you have spent years serving God.
And still there is a locked room in your heart you hope Jesus will never ask you to open.
He already knows what is inside.
And remarkably…
He has not stopped calling you.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not come merely to expose people like Solomon.
Jesus came to save sinners like Solomon.
And sinners like us.
The Bible ultimately refuses to let Solomon become our final king.
Israel needed someone greater.
Jesus Himself spoke of “something greater than Solomon.”
Solomon possessed wisdom.
Jesus Christ is the One in whom the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are found.
Solomon’s heart turned away.
Jesus perfectly obeyed His Father.
Solomon’s kingdom fractured.
Christ establishes a kingdom that will never finally be destroyed.
Solomon accumulated glory.
Jesus laid His glory aside, took the form of a servant, humbled Himself, and went obediently toward a cross.
Solomon’s disobedience helped tear a kingdom apart.
Christ allowed His own body to be torn so rebels could be reconciled to God.
Look at the scandal of the cross.
The innocent One condemned.
The Holy One surrounded by sinners.
Nails through hands that healed.
Blood running from the brow of the King of kings.
Jesus was not dying because He had lost control.
He was laying down His life.
For adulterers.
For idolaters.
For hypocrites.
For the sexually broken.
For religious pretenders.
For secret addicts.
For proud people.
For people whose hearts have wandered.
For people who knew better.
For people who promised God they would never do it again…
and did it again.
For us.
That is grace.
But biblical grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The cross proves precisely how serious sin is.
Grace is God doing for sinners what sinners could never do for themselves.
Christ bears sin.
Christ satisfies divine justice.
Christ offers forgiveness.
Christ calls sinners to repentance.
Christ gives new life.
So if Solomon’s story is exposing something inside you right now, do not waste the conviction by merely feeling emotional.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Name the thing.
Stop decorating what Jesus died to deliver you from.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Stop protecting the idol that is slowly eating your heart.
You do not need another hiding place.
You need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
Maybe you have wandered farther than you ever imagined you would.
Maybe you once burned for God.
Maybe worship once made you weep.
Maybe Scripture once felt alive.
Then something happened.
Pain.
Success.
Disappointment.
Lust.
Money.
A relationship.
Church hurt.
Pride.
Exhaustion.
Secret sin.
Slowly, almost invisibly, Jesus moved from the center of your attention toward the edge.
Come home.
Not because you can repair yourself.
Because Christ receives repentant sinners.
The Gospel is not “clean yourself up and perhaps Jesus will accept you.”
The Gospel announces that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
Repentance is not purchasing His mercy.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior whose mercy you desperately need.
Perhaps your scandal is different from Solomon’s.
Grace still knows your address.
If conviction is exposing something you need to surrender, you can simply write “Jesus, forgive me.”
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that we need Him becomes the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And if you need prayer, say it without shame:
“Pray for me.”
There are people reading this who may understand your battle more than you realize.
And if Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody.
Your testimony may become another person’s reason to believe that restoration is possible.
Someone else may desperately need to see those words tonight.
Then think about one person whose heart has been drifting.
Not ten people.
One.
The friend who stopped going to church.
The husband quietly struggling.
The wife carrying wounds nobody notices.
The son or daughter questioning everything.
The believer living two lives.
The person who thinks his or her sin has gone too far for Jesus.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
It does not.
But if biblical truth has strengthened you, sharing it can become a simple act of stewardship.
Your share may put Scripture in front of them at exactly the moment they are wondering whether God still wants them.
There may come a day when Solomon’s warning is no longer something you are reading about.
It may become something you desperately need to remember:
Guard your heart before the thing you love begins pulling your heart away from the One who loves you.
We want this community to be more than another stream of religious content.

We want people continually brought back to Jesus Christ—to Scripture, conviction, repentance, grace, forgiveness, healing, discipleship, spiritual nourishment, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
It does not purchase blessing.
It does not make someone a better Christian.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of stewarding resources for something you believe is helping people encounter biblical truth.
Pray.
Share.
Save the article.
Invite others into the community.
Because the goal was never simply to build an audience.
The goal is that Christ would be known.
That Scripture would be opened.
That wandering hearts would return.
That sinners would repent.
That wounded believers would discover they have not outrun the reach of Christ’s mercy.
That people trapped in darkness would hear the Gospel clearly.
That Jesus—not Solomon, not Gospel Warrior, not any preacher, ministry, author, platform, or personality—would receive the glory.
Solomon had wisdom, wealth, influence, women, palaces, servants, international recognition, and almost everything the human heart imagines will finally make it satisfied.
Yet none of it could safely occupy the place belonging to God.
Neither can your idol.
Neither can mine.
The question was:
Did God approve of Solomon’s many wives?
Scripture’s answer is no.
God had warned Israel’s king not to multiply wives precisely because his heart could turn away.
Solomon multiplied them anyway.
His heart turned.
His idolatry brought judgment.
But even that is not the final word of the Bible.
Because beyond Solomon stands another King.
A better King.
A faithful King.
A sinless King.
A crucified King.
A risen King.
Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the most beautiful difference between Solomon’s story and yours is this:
Your story is not finished simply because you wandered.
You can repent today.
You can come into the light today.
You can surrender the idol today.
You can confess the secret today.
You can return to Christ today.
You can stop defending the thing that is destroying you.
You can fall before the King who already knows the worst chapter and still calls sinners to Himself.
Maybe that is why this story survived for thousands of years.
Not so we could gossip about Solomon’s scandal.
So we could recognize our own hearts.
And then look beyond ourselves toward Jesus.
Solomon teaches us that extraordinary wisdom cannot save the human heart.
Only Christ can.
And when grace reaches the place you thought had ruined your story forever, the scandal no longer gets to write the ending.
The thing that turned your heart away from God does not have to have the final word—Jesus is still calling your heart home.
